197.title: Pauri 22, sound: paataalaa paataal
197.howItsDone: Pauri 22 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; its opening line, with its doubled words, has a rhythm that can be heard even before the meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hour creation began. Your line was only the maker knows. Today, Japji turns from when to where.

Stand in an elevator in a very tall building and look at the buttons. Basement, sub-basement, parking level three. Above you, floor after floor, up to a number you can barely read. Now imagine the buttons never end, in either direction. Below the lowest basement, another. Above the top floor, another sky. Yesterday Japji asked when. Today it asks where, and how far, and the first line of Pauri 22 sounds like that endless elevator.
screen: `AN ELEVATOR, BASEMENT TO SKY.` → `THE BUTTONS NEVER END.` → `FROM WHEN TO WHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in the original: paataalaa paataal lakh aagaasaa aagaas. Take it apart. Paataal, paa-TAAL: the lower worlds, the regions under the earth. Old Indian cosmology spoke of many of them, one below another. So paataalaa paataal: underworlds below underworlds. Lakh: a hundred thousand, the word Indians still use for big numbers, as in five lakh rupees. Aagaas, aa-GAAS: sky, the heavens, related to the Sanskrit akasha. Aagaasaa aagaas: skies beyond skies. Put together: underworlds below underworlds, and hundreds of thousands of skies above skies. Now listen to the build. Each half doubles its word. The first form, with the extra aa, reaches; the second lands. It sounds like going down a staircase, step after step, then climbing into the sky, step after step. The line doesn't describe the size of the universe. It lets the mouth do the measuring. It also carries on what the countless stanzas started, now with a direction. Asankh was about number. This is depth and height: down, down, up, up. The rest of the stanza asks whether anyone has found the end, and whether it could ever be written. That's tomorrow. Today, just the elevator, and its sound.
screen: `PAATAAL — THE LOWER WORLDS.` · `LAKH — A HUNDRED THOUSAND.` · `AAGAAS — SKY, SKIES BEYOND SKIES.` · `DOWN, DOWN, UP, UP.` · then, large: `PAATAALAA PAATAAL.`

segments.voice: Say the line aloud: paataalaa paataal, lakh aagaasaa aagaas. On the first half, let your attention sink into your seat, the floor, the ground beneath; on the second, let it rise to the crown of your head and the space above it. Say it twice more, then sit quietly between the two, the ground below and the open space above.
Paataal, the lower worlds beneath the earth. It opens paataalaa paataal, lakh aagaasaa aagaas: underworlds below underworlds, hundreds of thousands of skies above skies.
Your line: paataalaa paataal. Down without a bottom, up without a top. See you tomorrow.

198.title: Pauri 22, meaning: worlds beyond worlds
198.hook: underworlds beyond underworlds, skies beyond skies; if it could be written it would be, but the writing runs out (Japji 22)
198.howItsDone: Pauri 22 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs often cite its closing, that only the One knows Himself, when speaking of the limits of human description.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 22. Your line was paataalaa paataal: underworlds below underworlds, skies beyond skies. Today, what happens to anyone who tries to measure them.

Every notebook has a last page. Somebody sets out to list everything visible from a hilltop: each roof, each tree, each bird. The first notebook fills, then a shelf of them. The handwriting gets shaky, and the view hasn't gotten any smaller. The one writing runs out before the view does. Pauri 22 says something like that, and it isn't sad about it. It's almost relieved: this was never going to fit on paper.
screen: `LISTING EVERYTHING IN VIEW.` → `A NOTEBOOK, THEN A SHELF.` → `THE WRITER RUNS OUT FIRST.`

segments.voice: After the underworlds and the skies, Pauri 22 goes on, in paraphrase. People searched and searched for the farthest edge, and grew tired. The Vedas say this one thing: there's no end to find. The Kateb, the books of the Semitic traditions, speak of eighteen thousand worlds; but at the root there is one source. Notice what Guru Nanak does. He gathers the scriptures of the two communities around him, Hindu and Muslim, and hears them both pointing the same way: past counting, toward one. He doesn't set them against each other. Then the line behind today's carry: lekhaa hoe ta likheeai lekhai hoe vinaas. If there were an account, you could write it down; but the account perishes in the writing. Lekhaa is an account, a ledger, a tally. Vinaas is destruction, perishing. Commentators read it two ways: the account itself falls apart before it's done, or the one writing perishes before it's finished. Either way, the writing runs out. The stanza ends, in paraphrase: Nanak says, call Him great; He alone knows Himself. That's not giving up. It's the move Japji has made since Pauri 12, no pen for this, and it's the right size of a human being, standing under the sky. Anyone can say great. No one can write the whole ledger.
screen: `THEY SEARCHED, AND GREW TIRED.` · `THE VEDAS, THE KATEB, ONE SOURCE.` · `LEKHAA HOE TA LIKHEEAI.` · `CALL HIM GREAT; HE KNOWS HIMSELF.` · then, large: `THE WRITING RUNS OUT.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at the sky for a minute, through a window, from a doorway, or outside; if you can't see it, close your eyes and picture the widest sky you remember. Don't name or count what's there; just let it be bigger than you. Then close your eyes and sit with the size of it.
Lekhaa, an account or ledger. Worlds beyond worlds; the searchers grow tired; if it could be written, it would be, but the writing runs out. Call Him great.
Your line: the writing runs out. The ledger stays unfinished, and the sky is still there to look at. That's day one hundred ninety-eight.

199.title: Pauri 23, sound: saalaahee saalaah
199.hook: saalaahee saalaah etee surat na paaeeaa
199.tomorrow: Pauri 23, meaning: the ant who remembers
199.howItsDone: Pauri 23 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; praise, saalaah, is at the center of Sikh worship, sung as kirtan in gurdwaras every day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, worlds beyond worlds. Your line was the writing runs out. Today, the ones who praise.

A superfan of a band can recite every lyric and every tour. They've been to the shows, bought the records, worn the shirts. They praise and praise. Ask why the music moves them, though, and the answer often trails off into a shrug and a smile. The love is real; the explanation runs out. Praising something and fully grasping it aren't the same. Pauri 23 opens with the people who praise, and a gentle, honest line about what they still don't know.
screen: `A SUPERFAN.` → `THEY PRAISE AND PRAISE.` → `PRAISING ISN'T GRASPING.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in the original: saalaahee saalaah etee surat na paaeeaa. Slowly. Saalaah, saa-LAAH: praise. You met it in Pauri 19: akharee saalaah, through letters, praise. Saalaahee, saa-laa-HEE: the praisers, those who praise. So saalaahee saalaah: the praisers praise, the same root twice, like an echo. Etee: this much, so much. Surat: awareness, understanding, our word on day one hundred eighty-four, the waking attention that trust brings. Na paaeeaa: have not obtained, have not reached. Together: the praisers praise, but have not reached an understanding of how great. Hear the music. Saalaahee saalaah is soft and flowing, the long aa like breath going out. Then etee surat na paaeeaa tips over, as if it's shrugging. This isn't criticism of the people who praise; Japji is full of praise. It's the same honesty that runs through these stanzas: no pen for this, the writing runs out, only the Maker knows. Even the ones who praise most haven't grasped the size of it, and that's not a failure. Praise doesn't need a complete understanding to be real. Tomorrow the stanza gives a picture of that: rivers, the sea, and a very small ant.

segments.voice: Say the line aloud, saalaahee saalaah, etee surat na paaeeaa: once slowly, letting the long aa sounds breathe out, then twice more, softer each time. Sit and listen to the quiet after the last aa fades. Let the line keep echoing without working out what it means; that's tomorrow's job.
Saalaah, praise. It opens saalaahee saalaah, etee surat na paaeeaa: the praisers praise, but haven't grasped how great.
Your line: saalaahee. Admiring something doesn't have to wait until you can explain it. Until tomorrow.

200.title: Pauri 23, meaning: the ant who remembers
200.hook: rivers flow into the sea without knowing its size; kings with mountains of wealth are not equal to an ant who remembers (Japji 23)
200.howItsDone: Pauri 23 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs practice simran, remembering the Name through the day, and often quote the ant of this stanza to say remembrance matters more than wealth or rank.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 23. Your line was saalaahee: the praisers praise, but haven't grasped how great. Today, the stanza's meaning, and a very small hero.

Have you ever watched an ant for a whole minute? Get down low on a sidewalk and follow one. It carries a crumb twice its size, loses it, finds it, goes around a pebble, keeps going. It never looks up at the buildings or the traffic. It isn't impressed by anything. It just keeps its one thread. Now picture a king on a golden throne, with vaults of treasure and armies at the gate. Which one matters more? You'd probably laugh. Pauri 23 gives an answer that stops the laugh.
screen: `WATCH AN ANT FOR A MINUTE.` → `IT KEEPS ITS ONE THREAD.` → `THE ANT, OR THE KING?`

segments.voice: The stanza opened: the praisers praise, but haven't grasped how great. Now it gives two pictures. First, in paraphrase: rivers and streams pour into the ocean without knowing how big it is. They just flow in. That's anyone who praises: part of something they can't measure, pouring in anyway. The second picture turns the world's scale upside down. Kings and emperors, with kingdoms as vast as oceans and wealth piled like mountains, are not equal to an ant, if the ant does not forget the One in its heart. The word for ant is keeRee, one of the smallest living things anyone can see. And the condition is simple: je tis manahu na veesarahi, if it does not forget Him in its mind. The whole weight of the scale rests on that. The Sikh word for it is simran, remembrance, keeping the Name in mind through the day. Pauri 23 says a creature the size of a grain of rice, if it remembers, outweighs every palace. That doesn't make wealth evil; plenty of Sikhs run businesses and work hard. It says what the scale is actually measuring. Not size, not money, not how much you understand; the river doesn't understand the sea. Just whether you remember. And that closes this stretch of Japji: bhareeai hath, as you sow, teerath tap, only the Maker knows, worlds beyond worlds, the praisers, and now the ant. Two hundred days in, it's a good picture to carry: small, steady, remembering.
screen: `RIVERS DON'T KNOW THE SEA.` · `KINGS WITH MOUNTAINS OF WEALTH.` · `AN ANT WHO DOESN'T FORGET.` · `THE SCALE MEASURES REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `BE THE ANT.`

segments.voice: Watch something small: a leaf moving, a drop on a glass, a bug on the windowsill, or, if there's nothing, the small rise and fall of your own breath. Give it your whole attention, the way the ant gives its whole attention to one crumb. Each time your mind wanders off to bigger things, come back to the small one.
Simran, remembrance. Rivers pour into a sea they can't measure; kings with mountains of wealth don't equal an ant that remembers.
Your line: be the ant. Not the biggest on the scale, just the one who remembers. Day two hundred, done.

201.title: Pauri 24, sound: ant na siftee
201.hook: ant na siftee kahan na ant
201.tomorrow: Pauri 24, meaning: no end to praise
201.howItsDone: Pauri 24 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; its repeated word ant, end, gives the stanza a steady, rolling rhythm that many Sikhs know by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ant who remembers. Your line was be the ant. Today, a word that sounds just like it and means something else entirely.

Yesterday's hero was an ant. Today, the first word of Pauri 24 is ant too, spelled the same in English letters. In Punjabi, though, ant means end: the finish, the limit, the last page. And this stanza uses that word again and again, only to say there isn't one. No end, no end, no end. It's as if the whole stanza is a song about a road with no last mile. Today, just its first line, and the sound of it.
screen: `YESTERDAY, AN ANT.` → `TODAY, ANT MEANS END.` → `NO END, NO END, NO END.`

segments.voice: The first line, in the original: ant na siftee kahan na ant. Word by word. Ant, with a short a, UNT: end, limit. Na: no, not. Siftee, SIF-tee: praises, qualities. It comes from sifat, an Arabic word that traveled through Persian, meaning an attribute, a quality worthy of praise; Sikhs speak of sifat salaah, praise and glory. Kahan: saying, telling. So: no end to the praises, and no end to the telling of them. Now the shape. The line starts with ant and ends with ant. The word for end sits at both ends, like two bookends, and between them the line says there's no end. The shape plays against the meaning; that's poetry working before the meaning arrives. The rest of the stanza keeps going, in paraphrase: no end to His works, no end to His giving, no end to seeing, no end to hearing. Line after line, ant, and na. Guru Nanak is generally described as writing in the everyday speech of his region rather than a classical language, and his words draw on many sources: Punjabi, words from Sanskrit, words from Persian and Arabic, like sifat here. Tomorrow, what the whole stanza means. Today, the sound: end at both ends, and no end in the middle.
screen: `ANT — END, LIMIT.` · `SIFTEE — PRAISES, QUALITIES.` · `ANT AT BOTH ENDS OF THE LINE.` · `WORDS FROM MANY LANGUAGES.` · then, large: `ANT NA SIFTEE.`

segments.voice: Say the line aloud, ant na siftee, kahan na ant, and feel it start and finish on the same word; say it twice more, slower. Then sit with the breath: each one ends and another begins, and there's no last one you can feel coming. Rest in that rolling, one breath after another.
Siftee, praises. It opens ant na siftee, kahan na ant: no end to the praises, no end to their telling. Ant means end.
Your line: ant na siftee. The word for end, guarding a line with no end. See you tomorrow.

202.title: Pauri 24, meaning: no end to praise
202.hook: there is no end to His praise, His works, His gifts; the more is said, the more remains (Japji 24)
202.howItsDone: Pauri 24 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs often quote bahutaa aakheeai bahutaa hoe to say that praise of the One never runs out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 24. Your line was ant na siftee: end at both ends, and no end in the middle. Today, what the whole stanza says.

Thanking someone who really changed a life is harder than it sounds. A teacher, a grandparent, the friend who showed up when it mattered. You say thank you. Then you remember something else they did, and something else. You write a card, and the card's too small. The more you say, the more there is to say. That isn't a failure of your words; it's a sign of how much there was. Pauri 24 is built on that.
screen: `THANKING SOMEONE WHO CHANGED YOU.` → `ONE MORE THING, ONE MORE.` → `THE CARD IS TOO SMALL.`

segments.voice: Pauri 24 is a long chain of the word ant, end. In paraphrase: no end to the praises, no end to telling them. No end to His works, no end to His giving. No end to seeing, no end to hearing. His mind's purpose can't be known to its end. The created world can't be known to its end, nor its near shore, nor its far one. So many cry out wanting to find its limits, and its limits can't be found. No one knows this end. Then the line behind today's carry, in the original: bahutaa aakheeai bahutaa hoe. The more is said, the more there is. That's strange. Usually saying things uses them up; tell a story and it's told. Here every word of praise opens more to praise. Then the stanza climbs: great is the Master, high His place, and higher than high is His Name. Only someone as high as He could know Him; only He knows how great He is. And the last line: Nanak, the gift comes by the glance of grace. That's the stanza's quiet resting point. Talking can't reach the end. What anyone has comes as a gift, through nadar, grace, a word you'll keep meeting in Japji. So the praising never finishes, and that's not a problem to fix. In the stanza's terms, that's simply how praise of the endless works.
screen: `NO END TO WORKS, GIFTS, SEEING.` · `BAHUTAA AAKHEEAI BAHUTAA HOE.` · `HIGHER THAN HIGH, HIS NAME.` · `THE GIFT COMES BY GRACE.` · then, large: `THE MORE REMAINS.`

Nadar, grace, the glance that gives without being earned. No end to the praises, the works, the gifts; the more is said, the more there is; and the gift comes by grace.
Your line: the more remains. Like the card that's too small, it tells you how much there was. That's day two hundred two.

203.title: Pauri 25, sound: bahutaa karam
203.tomorrow: Pauri 25, meaning: even hunger is a gift
203.howItsDone: Pauri 25 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; the giving it describes is echoed in the langar, the free community kitchen of the gurdwara, where anyone is fed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no end to praise. Your line was the more remains. And that ends a week: paataalaa paataal, the endless elevator; the writing runs out; saalaahee, the praisers who never grasp it all; be the ant; ant na siftee, and the more remains. Every day, a way of saying: too big to measure.
screen: `NADAR — THE MORE REMAINS.` → `THE WEEK: ENDLESS, UNWRITTEN, THE ANT.`

segments.voice: A grandmother cooks for everyone who walks through her door. Plates keep coming out of the kitchen, and nobody gets a bill. Ask her how much she's made, and she laughs. She's never counted. Keeping score isn't how she thinks. Pauri 25 starts with a giver like that.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER WHO COOKS FOR ALL.` → `SHE'S NEVER COUNTED.` → `A GIVER LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: The first line, in the original: bahutaa karam likhiaa naa jaae. Bahutaa: so much, so great; you heard it yesterday in bahutaa aakheeai bahutaa hoe. Karam is a word to be careful with. It looks like karma, but Sikh commentators read karam here as a different word, from Persian and Arabic, meaning generosity, kindness, grace. Not what you've done, but what's given to you. Likhiaa: written. Naa jaae: cannot be. So: His generosity is so great it cannot be written down. That's the same honesty as the last few stanzas, the writing runs out, but now about giving. The next line, in paraphrase: the great Giver doesn't have even a sesame seed of greed. That's til again, the sesame seed from Pauri 21. The Giver wants nothing back, not even that much. Listen to the rhythm. Bahutaa karam: two strong beats, a lift. Likhiaa naa jaae: falling softly, like setting something down. Sikh practice has its own picture of a giver who doesn't count. The langar, the gurdwara's free kitchen, feeds anyone who comes, of any faith or none, sitting together on the floor, and nobody tallies who ate. Tomorrow the stanza goes somewhere surprising: to hunger and pain.
